newsitem.title: USA: W.House counsel downplays Clinton's legal troubles.
newsitem.headline: W.House counsel downplays Clinton's legal troubles.

text.p: Outgoing White House Counsel Jack Quinn on Saturday said he did not believe any of the legal cases involving President Bill Clinton posed a serious problem for the president.

Quinn, who announced his decision to return to private life this past week, said he was confident the array of legal issues facing Clinton, including an independent inquiry into the Whitewater land deal, would be cleared up relatively soon.

"We've had a lot of smoke to deal with, but not very many fires ... The smoke is beginning to clear and at the end of the day, which will come very soon, all of these issues will be resolved and we'll be able to look back and say this was a tempest in the teapot," Quinn told CNN's "Inside Politics."

He said the same was true about controversial fundraising by the Democratic National Committee, which had to return $2.5 million to various foreign contributors after reports that the contributions were improper.

"There is no way that any of this activity in any way, shape or form ever influenced the policy of the United States government, the decision-making by this president, by this vice president or by people in positions of responsibility within our administration," Quinn said.
Quinn also said he was surprised by the amount of speculation surrounding Clinton's decision Friday to ask Attorney General Janet Reno to stay on for his second term.

"I've been intimately involved... in the transition since weeks before the election, and I can tell you that the president never tasked out to us finding new leadership for the Department of Justice," Quinn said.

Reno, 58, whose future had been in doubt until Thursday night, faced White House complaints she was not a "team player" and sought too many special prosecutors to investigate the Whitewater affair involving the Clintons and other cases.
Quinn said Clinton was trying to avoid any suggestion that he was trying to affect Reno's decision on whether to ask an independent counsel to investigate the fundraising matter.

"No one meant for her to dangle in the wind, but in an abundance of caution the president decided that the ... cautious thing for him to do was to put off having his conversation with her, so that it under no circumstances could be interpreted as an effort to curry favour or in any way interfere with the decision she had to make," he said.
Quinn also reiterated his concerns about speeches made by Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr and said he would speak more openly after leaving the White House.

"The American people are entitled to know that the independent counsel is in fact independent annd that he is fair," Quinn said. "It gives me grave, grave concern when I see an independent counsel out making speeches about the subject matter of his inquiry."
